question: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents after she appeared to have a seizure at home. On presentation, she no longer has convulsions though she is still noted to be lethargic. She was born through uncomplicated vaginal delivery and was not noted to have any abnormalities at the time of birth. Since then, she has been noted by her pediatrician to be falling behind in height and weight compared to similarly aged infants. Physical exam reveals an enlarged liver, and laboratory tests reveal a glucose of 38 mg/dL. Advanced testing shows that a storage molecule present in the cells of this patient has abnormally short outer chains. Which of the following enzymes is most likely defective in this patient?

enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of a 3-month-old girl with lethargy, hypoglycemia (glucose of 38 mg/dL), failure to thrive, and an enlarged liver suggests a glycogen storage disease. The advanced testing indicating that the storage molecule has abnormally short outer chains is consistent with a deficiency in the branching enzyme, which is responsible for creating branches in glycogen. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of abnormal glycogen structures, characteristic of Andersen disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type IV). Other options, such as debranching enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, and phosphorylases, do not align with the specific findings of short outer chains in glycogen. Therefore, the most likely defective enzyme in this patient is the branching enzyme.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 3-month-old girl includes lethargy, hypoglycemia, failure to thrive, and hepatomegaly, which are indicative of a glycogen storage disease. The advanced testing revealing that the storage molecule has abnormally short outer chains suggests a defect in the branching enzyme, which is responsible for creating the branched structure of glycogen. In glycogen storage disease type IV (Andersen disease), there is a deficiency of the branching enzyme, leading to the accumulation of abnormal glycogen with short outer chains. Other options such as debranching enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, and phosphorylases do not correlate with the specific finding of short outer chains in glycogen. Therefore, the most likely defective enzyme in this patient is the branching enzyme. This reasoning aligns with the consensus in the medical literature regarding glycogen storage diseases.
